Highlights
Exact bounds over admissible values replace imputation for missing inputs.
Bounds were tested on real missingness in 26,057 external records.
Ranking matched linear regression; spline regression ranked slightly better.
At equal workload, bounds did not refer more cases than imputation.
PHQ-2 flagged 9.7% of adults; the prescreening model flagged 47.5%.
Abstract

*Background and objective:* Models that flag adults likely to score ≥ 10 on the Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9) from non-symptom information are judged mostly on discrimination, while incomplete records are left to imputation. We developed an interpretable fuzzy additive model whose admissible input values are declared in a machine-readable knowledge schema, and evaluated what exact bounds over those values add when inputs are missing.

*Methods:* NHANES 2017–March 2020 provided development (n = 5,793) and internal test (n = 2,483) data; August 2021–August 2023 (n = 5,455) and 2005–2014 (n = 26,057) served as temporal and external validation with frozen models. Fourteen non-symptom variables were mapped to 39 concepts with external cut-points. Algorithm 1 computes exact probability bounds over the admissible values of missing inputs; the system abstains when the bounds straddle the threshold. Algorithm 2 requests the missing input most likely to resolve an abstention. Comparators were logistic regression (linear, spline, sign-constrained; three missing-data strategies), GA²M and gradient-boosted trees. Bounds were evaluated on natural missingness, including free-day sleep absent for every external participant, and on random and non-random masking.

*Results:* External AUROC was 0.787 (0.778–0.797). It did not differ from logistic regression without missing indicators (0.787) and was 0.010 below spline regression (0.797); the protocol's primary comparison with indicator-based regression (0.779) reflects how that comparator handled the absent sleep variable. Externally, admissible-value bounds decided 69.2% of participants, against 56.4% for exact bounds of linear regression and none under complete-case abstention. At the same proportion referred, sensitivity was the same as for imputation-based models (94.6% versus 95.1%). Algorithm 2 needed 0.14 fewer inputs per abstention than a fixed order (0.11 to 0.17). PHQ-2 ≥ 3 flagged 9.7% of adults with sensitivity 0.687; the model flagged 47.5% with sensitivity 0.839.

*Conclusions:* The knowledge schema did not improve ranking. Exact bounds identified which decisions hold for every admissible value of the missing inputs, decided more records than linear bounds when a variable was structurally absent, and did not refer more cases at equal workload. The model may support record-based prioritisation where no symptom question can be asked; it is not a substitute for the PHQ-2.
*Keywords:* Depression screening; PHQ-9; Fuzzy rule-based systems; Missing data; Abstention; Interpretable machine learning; External validation; NHANES
1. Introduction

The PHQ-9 is a nine-item self-report instrument, and a total score of 10 or more is the most widely used threshold for elevated depressive symptoms [1, 2]. Its two-item short form, the PHQ-2, is the usual first step of two-stage screening [3, 4]. Anyone proposing an indirect model therefore has to answer a blunt question: why predict the score instead of asking two questions? The defensible use case is narrow. When no contact with the person has yet taken place, for example when a service reviews records or survey data to decide whom to invite for assessment, symptom questions cannot be asked, while age, sex, income, education, body mass index, chronic conditions, sleep duration and self-rated health may already be on file. A model on such data can prioritise who is asked to complete the questionnaire; it cannot replace it and it does not diagnose depression. Prevalence of elevated symptoms in United States adults has also risen over the past decade [5, 6], which makes behaviour across survey periods part of the question.

Several studies have used the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) to predict PHQ-9-defined depression from non-questionnaire variables, with logistic nomograms [7, 8] or machine-learning classifiers explained post hoc with SHAP values [9, 10]. A separate line of work has built fuzzy expert systems and fuzzy ontologies for depression [11–14]; these are interpretable by construction, but their inputs are symptom ratings, PHQ-9 answers or sensor streams. Between the two lines sits a well-developed family of inherently interpretable models for tabular data [15–17]: generalised additive models and their pairwise-interaction extension GA²M, implemented as the explainable boosting machine [18–21]; rule ensembles such as RuleFit [22]; sparse integer scoring systems [23]; and gradient-boosted trees with monotone constraints. A fuzzy rule system on non-symptom data has to be judged against this family, not only against black boxes.

Our earlier view was that a knowledge structure could improve inference itself. The data did not support that view (Section 3.4): with knowledge-based cut-points and sign priors, the fitted model is close to a sign-constrained piecewise-linear additive model, and it ranks people about as well as linear logistic regression. The more useful question concerns incomplete records. Routine pipelines impute silently, which hides how much a decision depends on what was not observed [24, 25]. Three lines of work address this. Credal classifiers treat missing values conservatively, compute predictions over all completions of a record and return an indeterminate output when the completions disagree [26, 27]. Pattern submodels fit a separate model for each missingness pattern and so avoid imputation at prediction time [28]. Active feature acquisition chooses at test time which unobserved feature to acquire next [29]. Interval-valued fuzzy aggregation [30] and exact bounds of weighted averages under interval weights [31, 32] are related ideas from fuzzy systems. Our approach is closest to the credal view: it bounds the prediction of a fitted additive model over declared admissible values and abstains when the bound contains the threshold, and it adds a simple acquisition rule driven by those bounds. Its specific features are that admissible values are declared per variable in a released schema, that the bounds are exact for an additive rule class with piecewise-linear memberships, and that both are tested on real, structured missingness.

This study asks three questions. (RQ1) How does a knowledge-schema-constrained fuzzy additive model compare with linear, spline and sign-constrained logistic regression, GA²M and gradient-boosted trees in discrimination, calibration and net benefit, internally, in a later survey period and in earlier survey cycles? (RQ2) Which design choices carry measurable value: rule structure, aggregation, fuzzy memberships, knowledge-based cut-points or sign constraints? (RQ3) When inputs are missing, under natural and simulated missingness, what do exact admissible-value bounds and bound-guided acquisition add over imputation, missing indicators, multiple imputation, linear bounds and complete-case abstention, including at an equal proportion referred?

The contributions are as follows. (i) A knowledge schema in four layers (observation, concept, rule, provenance), released as a JSON-LD file with a SKOS concept scheme, which declares each variable's admissible range, each concept's membership function and cut-point source, and sign priors estimated on an independent survey cycle. (ii) Algorithm 1, exact bounds of the predicted probability over all admissible completions of a record, for additive rule models with one- and two-concept antecedents; we prove exactness for components with up to two continuous missing variables. For the recommended main-effects model the computation reduces to a separable search over each variable's breakpoints; the propositions matter for the general rule class. (iii) Algorithm 2, a bound-guided rule for which missing input to request. (iv) An evaluation in three survey periods against seven comparators, with the PHQ-2 as a reference point, and of the bounds under natural missingness, non-random masking and matched workload. We report the development history, including an abandoned first version, and make no claim of clinical utility.
2. Materials and methods
2.1. Study design, intended use and reporting

This is a retrospective development, temporal and external validation study of a prediction model, reported following TRIPOD+AI [33] (checklist in Appendix B). The intended user is a service that reviews existing survey or record information before any symptom questionnaire has been administered; the intended action is to recommend completing the PHQ-9 or an equivalent assessment. Where a person can be asked two questions, the PHQ-2 is the appropriate first step, and we report it as a reference point (Section 2.13). The model does not diagnose major depressive disorder, does not estimate future incidence and is not a tool for assessing self-harm risk. Predictors and outcome are measured in the same survey, so the target is concurrent elevated symptoms.
2.2. Data sources

NHANES is a continuous cross-sectional survey of the non-institutionalised United States population. Development data came from the 2017–March 2020 pre-pandemic release, which combines the 2017–2018 cycle with data collected until fieldwork was suspended in March 2020 [34]; 2017–2018 therefore cannot serve as independent validation. Temporal validation used August 2021–August 2023, and external validation the five two-year cycles 2005–2006 to 2013–2014. The 2015–2016 cycle was used only to estimate direction priors (Section 2.6). Components were merged by the respondent identifier SEQN: demographics, depression screener, sleep, body measures, hospital utilisation, smoking, physical activity, medical conditions, diabetes and blood pressure questionnaires.
2.3. Participants and outcome

We included respondents aged ≥ 18 years with valid responses (0–3) to all nine PHQ-9 items (DPQ010–DPQ090) [35]. Refused, don't-know and missing responses were not treated as symptom values; DPQ100 (functional difficulty) is not part of the total. With q_{ij} the response of participant i to item j,

All PHQ-9 items, the total score and any derived quantity were excluded from the predictors. Of 9,693 adults in 2017–March 2020, 1,385 had no depression screener record and 32 had at least one invalid item, leaving 8,276 participants (767 with PHQ-9 ≥ 10, 9.3%). Of 8,153 adults in 2021–2023, 2,634 had no screener record and 64 an invalid item, leaving 5,455 (723 positive, 13.3%). In 2005–2014, 4,082 of 30,295 adults had no screener record and 156 an invalid item, leaving 26,057 (2,294 positive, 8.8%) (Fig. 1). Included and excluded participants are compared in Table A4. The development release was split 70/30 at participant level, stratified by outcome (seed 2026), into a development set (n = 5,793) and an internal test set (n = 2,483).

Candidate predictors had to be plausibly available before a symptom questionnaire, clearly defined, not derived from the outcome, and fielded with the same coding in 2017–2020 and 2021–2023. Fourteen variables qualified: age, sex, family income-to-poverty ratio, education (five levels), marital status (married/partnered, previously married, never married), body mass index, usual sleep duration on workdays and on free days, self-rated general health (five levels), current smoking, doctor-told diabetes, doctor-told hypertension, daily sedentary time, and a count of ten doctor-told chronic conditions (asthma, arthritis, congestive heart failure, coronary heart disease, angina, myocardial infarction, stroke, liver condition, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, cancer). All are survey items. Several would not be found in a typical electronic health record: self-rated health, sleep duration and sedentary time are interview questions, and the chronic conditions are self-reported 'doctor-told' answers rather than coded diagnoses. Table 2 marks which variables are usually available as structured record data, and Section 2.13 describes a model restricted to them.

Contact with a mental health professional was not used, because it is close to the outcome. Race and ethnicity served only for subgroup evaluation. Two sleep items with strong associations in the earlier cycle (SLQ050, SLQ120) were not fielded in 2021–2023 and were examined only in a development-period sensitivity analysis. Sleep duration overlaps conceptually with the PHQ-9 sleep item but is collected by a separate questionnaire; we report an analysis without sleep variables. In the development set 20.0% of participants had at least one missing predictor, mostly income-to-poverty ratio (13.3%).

The 2005–2014 cycles required three harmonisation decisions, written into the analysis protocol (Section 2.8) before the files were downloaded: workday sleep came from SLD010H, recorded in whole hours; free-day sleep was not collected and was missing for every external participant; and the chronic-condition count used the nine items available before the COPD item was introduced in 2013–2014. Sedentary time was not collected in 2005–2006. Two routine recodings were made when the files were read (marital status mapped to the three categories above; race and ethnicity before 2011 from RIDRETH1, which has no separate Asian category). Variables absent in a cycle were left missing for every model.
2.5. Knowledge schema

We use the term knowledge schema rather than ontology, because no description-logic reasoner [36] is involved and the structure is a typed, versioned declaration rather than an axiomatised theory. It has four layers (Fig. 2). The observation layer declares each variable with its domain, type, unit, NHANES source field and admissible range (Table 2; Table A5). The concept layer holds 39 linguistic concepts (fuzzy sets [37]), each bound to exactly one variable. The rule layer stores antecedent–coefficient pairs with their sign constraints. The provenance layer records the source of each cut-point and each prior. The schema is distributed as a JSON-LD 1.1 file [38] in which concepts are SKOS concepts [39] of one concept scheme, with membership functions, priors and rules as typed nodes; the file is loaded by the model code, so the released artefact is the one that produced the results.

2.6. Direction priors from an independent cycle

For each concept we estimated, in NHANES 2015–2016 (n = 5,134, 415 positive), the risk ratio of PHQ-9 ≥ 10 for membership ≥ 0.5 versus < 0.5 with a log-scale 95% confidence interval; the direction D(k) was +1 if the lower limit exceeded 1, −1 if the upper limit was below 1, and 0 otherwise. The procedure estimated 17 positive, 16 negative and 8 neutral directions for the 39 concepts other than free-day sleep and the five extended-sleep concepts (Table A1). Free-day sleep was not asked in 2015–2016, so its 3 concepts inherited the direction of the workday concepts; these priors were never estimated and are marked in Tables 2 and 3. Each prior compares a concept with all other values of its variable, whereas each coefficient of the main-effects model (Section 2.7) is a contrast with one reference concept. A sign constraint therefore restricts a different estimand from the one the prior measured. We report the consequences in three sensitivity analyses: priors from age- and sex-adjusted models, priors from one mutually adjusted model, and priors estimated for the reference contrast actually fitted (concept versus reference concept).
2.7. Model: sign-constrained fuzzy additive rules
A rule r has an antecedent A_r of one or two concepts and fires with strength
μ_r(x) = min_{k ∈ A(r)} μ_k(x_k).

A two-concept antecedent must refer to two different variables, and the non-zero directions of its concepts must agree; the rule inherits the common direction s_r ∈ {−1, 0, +1}. Rules combine additively on the log-odds scale,
η(x) = logit p(x) = β_0 + Σ_{r=1}^{R} β_r μ_r(x),   subject to s_r β_r ≥ 0,

a zero-order Takagi–Sugeno system [43] with log-odds consequents. In the selected structure every single-concept rule enters except one reference concept per variable (the concept with the highest mean membership in development data), and K two-concept rules may then be added greedily by the score statistic g_r²/h_r, with g_r = Σ_i μ_{ir}(y_i − p_i) and h_r = Σ_i μ_{ir}² p_i(1 − p_i), provided the sign of g_r is compatible with s_r and the rule's firing vector does not correlate above 0.95 with a selected rule. Coefficients were fitted by L-BFGS-B on the ridge-penalised log-likelihood (λ = 10⁻³) with the sign constraints as box bounds. During fitting, and for the point score, a missing membership was replaced by its development-sample mean. With Ruspini partitions the single-concept part is a piecewise-linear additive function of each continuous variable with knots at the schema's cut-points, i.e. a constrained generalised additive model [18] whose terms carry names, and two-concept rules play the role of GA²M interactions [19]. K was chosen from {0, 8, 16, 32, 64} by 5-fold cross-validated AUROC in the development set, taking the smallest K within 0.005 of the best. Cross-validated AUROC was 0.759, 0.756, 0.760, 0.754 and 0.759 (logistic regression 0.761), so K = 0: the final model has 25 single-concept rules and an intercept.

The structure above is the second version of the system. Version 1 selected K = 32 rules of any arity by the same greedy procedure with no forced main effects; 30 of its 32 rules were two-concept conjunctions. On the internal and temporal sets it trailed logistic regression by 0.023 (−0.043 to −0.003) and 0.012 (−0.025 to −0.000) AUROC. We attributed the gap to the absence of main effects, tested that diagnosis with development-set cross-validation only, and wrote a protocol fixing the revised structure, the K grid and selection rule, the comparators and ablations of the first submission, the external cohorts and their harmonisation, and the primary comparison (external AUROC versus logistic regression with missing indicators). 2.9. Algorithm 1: exact admissible-value bounds
Let O and M be the observed and missing variables of a person. Instead of imputing x_M, the system reports the range of probabilities the model can produce for any admissible completion,
p_L = min σ(η(x_O, x_M)),   p_U = max σ(η(x_O, x_M)),   over x_M ∈ 𝒳_M,

where 𝒳_M is the product of the admissible sets declared in the observation layer (category sets for discrete variables, intervals for continuous ones; Table A5). Because σ is monotone it suffices to bound η. Each rule involves at most two variables, so η is a constant plus a sum of functions of connected components of missing variables (two missing variables are connected if a rule contains both), and the extrema of η are sums of per-component extrema. Algorithm 1 (Box 1) computes them exactly.

*Proposition 1 (one continuous missing variable).* Let x ∈ [l, u] be the only continuous missing variable of a component, with all discrete variables of the component fixed. Then g(x) = Σ_r β_r min(μ_{k(r)}(x), c_r), where c_r ∈ [0, 1] is the observed partner membership of rule r (c_r = 1 for single-concept rules). Each μ_k is continuous and piecewise linear with breakpoints at its trapezoid corners, and min(μ_k(x), c_r) adds breakpoints only where μ_k(x) = c_r, i.e. at x = a + c_r(b − a) and x = d − c_r(d − c). Hence g is continuous and piecewise linear on [l, u] with breakpoints in the finite set 𝒞 = {l, u} ∪ {corners} ∪ {solutions of μ_k(x) = c_r}. A continuous piecewise-linear function on a closed interval attains its extrema at an endpoint or a breakpoint, so min g and max g are attained on 𝒞 and enumerating 𝒞 is exact. □

*Proposition 2 (two continuous missing variables).* Let (x, z) ∈ [l_x, u_x] × [l_z, u_z] be connected through pair rules min(μ_k(x), μ_m(z)). Partition each axis at its breakpoints from Proposition 1. On each resulting rectangle every membership is affine, so each pair term equals one of two affine functions, switching along the line μ_k(x) = μ_m(z). These lines cut the rectangle into convex polygons on which F(x, z) is affine; F is continuous, so its extrema over the rectangle lie at polygon vertices. Every vertex is a rectangle corner, an intersection of a switching line with a rectangle edge, or an intersection of two switching lines inside the rectangle. Enumerating these points on all rectangles is exact. □

Discrete variables in a component are enumerated over their categories, and Propositions 1–2 are applied for each combination. Components with more than two continuous missing variables fall back to the box bound obtained by letting each missing membership range over [0, 1]; this is a valid outer bound, not an exact one, and we report how often it occurs. For a component with m_c categorical combinations, n_b breakpoints per axis and q pair rules, the cost is O(m_c n_b) evaluations for one continuous variable and O(m_c n_b² q²) for two. For the selected main-effects model every component is a single variable with no partner, 𝒞 reduces to the trapezoid corners and range ends, and the bounds are exact. The first submission used a 41-point grid augmented with trapezoid corners; we compare it with Algorithm 1 in Section 3.6. The box bound, which ignores that memberships of one variable are linked through the partition, is retained as an ablation. For sign-constrained linear regression the analogous exact bound is closed-form: each missing input moves η linearly, so its extremes are at the ends of the admissible range, and marital status is enumerated over its categories.

Two remarks place Algorithm 1 in context. First, for the recommended main-effects model every rule involves one variable and has no partner, so η is a sum of univariate piecewise-linear functions and its bounds follow from evaluating each term at its breakpoints and range ends; this is elementary. Propositions 1 and 2 are needed for rule bases with conjunctions (version 1 and the interaction variant), and we present them as covering the general rule class, not as a property of the deployed model. Second, the same separable bounds hold for any logistic model whose terms are piecewise linear with constant tails at the same knots; a spline or linear model with unbounded tails gives bounds that grow with the admissible range. Whatever coverage advantage the proposed bounds have over linear bounds (Section 3.6) therefore comes from bounded basis functions, which the schema supplies through saturating memberships, not from the schema as such.

2.10. Algorithm 2: bound-guided input acquisition

An abstention means that at least one missing input could change the decision. Algorithm 2 asks for one missing input at a time. For each candidate input v, it estimates the probability that observing v alone resolves the decision, ρ_v = Σ_j w_{vj} 1[p_L(x_O, v = v_j) ≥ t or p_U(x_O, v = v_j) < t], where the other missing inputs remain unknown and v_j, w_{vj} are support points and weights of the development-set distribution of v (all categories for discrete variables, 25 quantile points for continuous ones). The input with the largest ρ_v is requested, its value is entered, the bounds are recomputed, and the loop stops when the decision is resolved or no missing input remains. Using the marginal distribution ignores what the observed inputs say about v. A conditional version would draw the support points from the distribution of v given x_O, for example from the chained-equation imputation model fitted for the comparators; ρ_v would then favour inputs whose likely values, for this person, fall on one side of the threshold. We compared the marginal rule with three orders: a fixed order by the range of each input's total log-odds contribution, a cost order that requests structured record items first (diabetes, hypertension, chronic conditions, BMI, smoking, marital status, education), then income, then interview items (self-rated health, sleep, sedentary time), and a random order. Evaluation used internal test records with 10% or 30% of inputs masked at random and temporal records with 30% masked; a requested masked input was revealed with its true value, and inputs missing in the original data could not be revealed. Differences in the number of inputs requested are paired by record, with bootstrap intervals (2,000 resamples). By construction every order resolves the same records with the same final decisions.
2.11. Explanation trace

For each person the system exports a JSON trace with the inputs, missing-input flags, the membership of every concept used by the rule base and its provenance, each rule's firing strength (or lower and upper firing when an input is missing), coefficient and log-odds contribution β_r μ_r, the intercept, the probability bounds and, for abstentions, the input requested by Algorithm 2. For complete inputs the contributions add exactly to η. This additive decomposition holds for any generalised linear model, so it is not by itself an advantage over logistic regression; Section 3.7 compares the two on size and sign plausibility instead.
2.12. Comparators and ablations

Comparators were logistic regression with median imputation, missing-value indicators, standardisation and an L2 penalty chosen over ten values by 5-fold cross-validated AUROC; gradient-boosted trees [45] (scikit-learn HistGradientBoostingClassifier [46], native missing-value routing, minimum leaf size 50, tuned over learning rate, depth and iterations; learning_rate=0.03, max_depth=2, max_iter=300 selected); logistic regression with median imputation and no indicators; logistic regression after multiple imputation by chained equations [47] (five imputations with posterior draws, predictions averaged); logistic regression with restricted cubic splines [48] (four knots at the 5th, 35th, 65th and 95th development percentiles) for age, BMI and both sleep durations, other inputs linear, median imputation without indicators; sign-constrained logistic regression on the raw inputs, with the direction priors imposed on main effects (age, BMI and sleep unconstrained because their associations are U-shaped; λ = 0.01); an explainable boosting machine (GA²M; interpret 0.7.8, 10 pairwise interactions, missing values in a separate bin) [19, 21]; and gradient-boosted trees with monotone constraints derived from the same priors. Rule ensembles [22] and integer scoring systems [23] were not fitted. Bounds for the spline model were computed by a dense 2,001-point search per missing input, which is exact up to the grid because the model is additive in its inputs. Version-level comparators were version 1 (K = 32), main effects plus 16 pair rules, and normalised zero-order TSK aggregation p = Σ_r w_r μ_r c_r / Σ_r w_r μ_r (K = 32), which also differs in rule filtering, gain and point score. Single-element ablations were: no direction constraints; crisp memberships; quantile-based memberships with no constraints and median imputation ('fuzzy without schema'); median imputation instead of bounds; and box bounds.
2.13. Performance measures and secondary analyses

Every model produced out-of-fold predictions in the development set by 5-fold cross-validation. These were used to fit a Platt recalibration map and to fix the referral threshold as the largest score reaching an out-of-fold sensitivity of at least 0.80. Models were then refitted on the whole development set and applied unchanged to all cohorts. We report AUROC, area under the precision–recall curve (AUPRC), sensitivity, specificity, predictive values, proportion flagged, Brier score, calibration slope and observed-to-expected ratio (O/E) [49], and net benefit across threshold probabilities 0.02–0.30 [50, 51]. Confidence intervals came from 1,000 bootstrap resamples (500 for AUROC in single cycles); AUROC differences used 2,000 paired resamples (1,000 in single cycles) with percentile intervals and two-sided bootstrap p-values. The primary comparison is external AUROC of the proposed model versus logistic regression; all other comparisons are secondary and unadjusted for multiplicity, so we interpret them by effect size and interval width rather than by p < 0.05. AUROC weighted by NHANES interview weights is a sensitivity analysis.

The bootstrap resamples the test set only. To include training variability, the proposed model, version 1, the interaction variant, three ablations and five comparators were refitted on 20 repeated stratified 70/30 splits of the full 2017–2020 release, with hyperparameters fixed at the values selected above. Recalibration-in-the-large was examined by estimating an intercept shift on a random half of the temporal or external cohort and evaluating O/E, Brier score, sensitivity, specificity and proportion flagged on the other half (200 repetitions). Operating points are also expressed per 1,000 adults as questionnaires avoided and cases missed.

The PHQ-2 reference used items DPQ010 and DPQ020 with the usual cut-point ≥ 3 [3, 4]; it is not a competitor in the same input space but shows what two symptom questions achieve. A record-typical model used only age, sex, BMI, diabetes, hypertension, chronic-condition count, smoking, education and marital status (and a seven-variable version without the last two). Direction priors were re-estimated with age- and sex-adjusted and with mutually adjusted logistic models, and the proposed model and version 1 refitted with them.

Missing inputs were examined in three settings. Natural missingness: all models were applied to the internal, temporal and external cohorts as observed; externally free-day sleep is absent for everyone and sedentary time in 2005–2006, and income-to-poverty ratio is missing for 7.5–13.3% of participants in every cohort. Simulated missingness completely at random (MCAR) on the internal test set: each of the 12 predictors other than age and sex masked with probability 10–50% (10 repetitions; the same masks for every model and analysis), or whole domains removed. Missingness not at random (MNAR): income-to-poverty ratio masked with probability 0.6 if below 1.3 and 0.1 otherwise, self-rated health masked with probability 0.6 if fair or poor and 0.1 otherwise, or both (10 repetitions). For every model we report AUROC and, at its frozen threshold, sensitivity, specificity and proportion flagged. For models with bounds (the proposed model, its box-bound ablation, sign-constrained and spline regression) we report coverage, abstention, decisions on covered cases and refer-on-abstain operating characteristics, and add a complete-case baseline that abstains whenever any input is missing. Because refer-on-abstain and a point-score threshold refer different numbers of people, decision value was compared at matched workload, setting each point-score model's threshold so that it flagged the same proportion as the proposed refer-on-abstain policy, and by net benefit at threshold probabilities 0.05 and 0.10. Coverage was recomputed with continuous ranges narrowed to the 1st–99th development percentiles. A further sensitivity analysis refitted every model without free-day sleep and evaluated it externally, to show how the treatment of a structurally absent variable affects the primary comparison. Subgroup AUROC, sensitivity and O/E were computed by sex, age band and race and ethnicity where at least 10 positive cases were available.
2.14. Software and use of generative AI in the research process

Analyses used Python 3.13 with pandas 3.0.5, scikit-learn 1.9.1, SciPy 1.18.1, statsmodels and interpret 0.7.8. The analysis code was written with the assistance of a generative AI tool (Claude, Anthropic), which drafted the cohort construction, model, Algorithms 1–2, experiments and figure scripts under the authors' specification. The authors reviewed the code, and correctness was checked by tests that do not depend on the generated code: the cohort flow and direction priors were reproduced exactly from the public files; Algorithm 1 was checked against dense brute-force evaluation (4,001-point grids) and against the earlier grid implementation; traces were re-evaluated by independent code; and the full pipeline was re-run from raw files, reproducing every reported number of the first submission. All numbers in this manuscript are written by the analysis code to one statistics file and inserted programmatically. The code, schema and statistics file are available for review (Code availability).

4. Discussion
4.1. Principal findings

For RQ1, the proposed model ranked people about as well as linear logistic regression in all three periods and slightly less well than spline regression in every period and than GA²M on 2017–2023 data. The primary comparison favoured it only because the comparator handled a structurally absent variable with an indicator; against regression without indicators there was no difference. Calibration in earlier cycles held for every regression model without indicators and failed for every model that learnt a missing-value route. For RQ2, rule structure had the largest effect: conjunctive rule bases and normalised TSK aggregation transported worse. Fuzzy memberships gave a small, consistent advantage over crisp ones; knowledge-based cut-points and sign constraints did not change ranking. For RQ3, exact bounds separated decisions that hold for every admissible value of the missing inputs from those that do not. They decided more records than linear bounds when a variable was absent for everyone or missing preferentially in high-risk records, fewer when the missing variables entered the linear model with small slopes, and they did not find more cases than imputation at equal workload.
4.2. What the knowledge schema contributes, and what it does not

The selected model is, mathematically, a sign-constrained piecewise-linear generalised additive model with knots at the schema's cut-points, and its discrimination is that of the regression family. We state this plainly because it relocates the contribution. The first submission attributed gains to the ontology; the revised analyses do not support that, and we have withdrawn the claim. Removing the schema as a whole, or any of its parts, left ranking within noise. The sign priors agreed with every unconstrained estimate of the main-effects model. They mattered only for the conjunctive version 1, where they pruned incoherent conjunctions; in that setting univariable priors led to better external discrimination than mutually adjusted ones, which suggests that a prior used to filter a search need not be the adjusted effect that a clinician would quote.

What the schema does contribute is the information that Algorithms 1 and 2 need and that a fitted model does not carry: the admissible set of each variable and, through saturating memberships, bounded terms. Bounded terms are what make the external bounds narrow; a spline model with constant tails at the same knots would share this property, so the advantage belongs to bounded basis functions rather than to the schema itself. A second, practical contribution is auditability. Each of the 25 terms is a named concept with a declared cut-point source and prior, released as a machine-readable file that the code loads, so a reader can check a coefficient against its declaration. The declarations have limits that the audit exposes: priors were estimated as concept versus all other values while coefficients are contrasts with a reference concept. Re-estimating the priors for the fitted contrast changed 4 directions (HighSedentary versus ModerateSedentary + to 0; LowSedentary versus ModerateSedentary − to 0; NormalWeight versus Obese 0 to −; OneChronicCondition versus NoChronicCondition 0 to +) and moved no coefficient by more than 0.0004. This is in line with interpretability criteria for fuzzy systems [54], but it is a property of documentation, not of accuracy.
4.3. Missing data, abstention and acquisition

Imputation and missing indicators produce a number for everyone and hide how much it depends on what was not observed. Bounds do not depend on the missingness mechanism: a decision that holds for every admissible value holds whatever the reason a value is missing. This is their main advantage, and the external cohort and the non-random masking scenarios show it in practice. It is a guarantee about individual decisions, not a gain in classification: at equal workload the bounds-based policy found as many cases as imputation, not more, and refer-on-abstain refers many people when much is missing. Algorithm 2 reduces that cost by asking for the input most likely to settle a decision; its advantage over a model-derived fixed order is small and over a record-consultation order moderate. Credal classifiers [26, 27] apply the same conservative logic to probabilistic classifiers, pattern submodels [28] avoid imputation by fitting one model per pattern, and learned acquisition policies [29] optimise the order of questions with more data than ours. A comparison with these methods on the same data is outside the scope of this study. Algorithm 1 applies to any additive model with piecewise-linear terms and at most pairwise interactions, including GA²M shape functions, and Algorithm 2 to any model with exact bounds.
4.4. Transport across survey periods

All models under-predicted in 2021–2023 by a similar factor, and a single intercept shift repaired it. NHANES documentation records several changes after the pandemic suspension that plausibly contributed: the depression screener moved from an interviewer-administered computer-assisted interview to audio computer-assisted self-interview [55], a mode change known to increase reporting of sensitive symptoms [56]; oversampling by race, Hispanic origin and income was discontinued [57]; and unweighted interview and examination response rates (all ages, including the screener response) fell to 34.5% and 25.6% from 51.0% and 46.9% in 2017–March 2020 [58, 59]. We cannot separate these from a real rise in prevalence [5], but the self-administration change alone is reason enough to expect a model trained on interviewer-administered data to under-predict. The loss of discrimination in 2021–2023 was shared by every model class and is consistent with the same changes. Any deployment would require local recalibration and monitoring regardless of model type [49].
4.5. Practical relevance

The model's use case is narrower than the first submission implied. With the full predictor set, which includes self-rated health, sleep and sedentary time asked in an interview, it flagged about half of adults to find about five in six with elevated symptoms; the PHQ-2 flagged about one in ten and found about two in three. With record-typical predictors alone, discrimination in the later period was modest. The model may therefore be useful for prioritising whom to invite when a survey or registry already holds self-rated health and lifestyle items but no symptom questions; it is not a substitute for asking the PHQ-2. Whether a prioritisation step of this kind saves effort in a real service, and whether its explanations help staff decide whom to contact, has not been evaluated.
4.6. Limitations

The revised model was designed after version-1 results on the internal and temporal sets had been seen, and the protocol that fixed it was not registered; the only record that it preceded the external download is a pair of file modification times, which cannot be verified independently. All comparators and analyses added during revision were specified after the original results were known. The external cohort is earlier cycles of the same survey, not a different health system. The outcome is a questionnaire threshold, not a diagnostic interview [2]. Predictors and outcome are cross-sectional; a trace explains the model, not the person's depression. Most predictors are survey self-reports. Algorithm 1 is exact for components with at most two continuous missing variables and uses an outer bound otherwise; the spline comparator's bounds use a dense grid. Algorithm 2 uses the marginal development distribution of each input and was evaluated by revealing masked values, which assumes that a requested input can be obtained. Credal classifiers, pattern submodels, learned acquisition policies, rule ensembles and integer scoring systems were discussed but not fitted. No clinician evaluated the explanations. Subgroup analyses were descriptive and underpowered for several groups.
5. Conclusions

A fuzzy additive model constrained by a knowledge schema ranked adults by the likelihood of elevated depressive symptoms about as well as linear logistic regression across three survey periods and slightly less well than spline regression; its knowledge-related elements did not improve discrimination. Its declared admissible values allow exact probability bounds that show which decisions hold whatever the missing inputs are, including when a variable is absent for everyone, and a bound-guided choice of which input to ask for next. At equal workload these bounds did not find more cases than imputation. Two symptom questions remain far more efficient than any non-symptom model where they can be asked.
